JUSTICE <note>original: "IVSTICIA"</note>
PRUDENCE <note>original: "PRVDEN," an abbreviation for *Prudencia*</note>
FORTITUDE <note>original: "FORTITV," an abbreviation for *Fortitudo*</note>
TEMPERANCE <note>original: "TEMPER," an abbreviation for *Temperantia*</note>

<note>This cover is a classic example of a 16th-century <term>blind-stamped</term> binding—a technique where heated metal rollers or individual stamps are pressed into dampened leather (usually pigskin or vellum) to create a permanent recessed design without using gold leaf or ink. 

The decorative borders here feature a repeating pattern of the four "Cardinal Virtues." In the Renaissance, these virtues—Justice, Prudence, Fortitude (or Strength), and Temperance (or Moderation)—were considered the pillars of a moral life and were frequently used to decorate scholarly and religious volumes to reflect the wisdom contained within. The heavy brass and iron clasps on the edge were functional as well as decorative, designed to keep the parchment or paper pages flat and protected from humidity.</note>

<summary>This page describes the ornate 16th-century pigskin binding of the manuscript, featuring stamped allegorical figures of the four Cardinal Virtues. The binding style and iconography suggest a work of significant scholarly or moral value from the Renaissance period.</summary>

<keywords>bookbinding, 16th century, Cardinal Virtues, Justice, Prudence, Fortitude, Temperance, blind-stamping, pigskin, vellum, Renaissance iconography</keywords>

Before modern textbooks, children used these to learn their alphabets and basic prayers.</note>

<note>This text is a variation of the Latin proverb: *Radix amara eruditionis, dulcis fructus*, meaning "The root of learning is bitter, but the fruit is sweet." It suggests that while the process of study is difficult, the knowledge gained is rewarding. The words are woven into the branches of a "Tree of Knowledge."</note>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues from the title leaf of the 1519 Aldine edition of Homer. While the previous page contained handwritten owner inscriptions and a quote from Horace, this page contains the formal printed dedication by the publisher, Aldus Manutius, to the scholar Girolamo Aleandro (Hieronymus Aleandrus).</meta>

# ALDUS PIUS MANUTIUS THE ROMAN
# TO GIROLAMO ALEANDRO
# OF MOTTA, SENDS FONDEST GREETINGS.

If there is anyone who accuses us because we dedicate the books of others to this or that person according to our own whim—even though I recall writing in another letter why I feel I am in some way entitled to do this, so that the reason might be known from there—nevertheless, let him also read here, if he pleases, and cease his slandering. For since books seem to be born again, in a sense, within our household, shaped with the greatest care and the greatest labors, I believe I am permitted <note>original: "διὰ τὴν τοιαύτην παλιγγενεσίαν," meaning "on account of such a rebirth or regeneration"</note> through such a rebirth to dedicate them to whomever I please. Therefore, we wished the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* of Homer, along with the other extant works by the same poet, to go forth from our New Academy <note>The *Neacademia* was Aldus's circle of scholars in Venice who spoke only Greek during their meetings.</note> under your name, my dear Aleandro. We do this not so that we might make you more eager for the study of refined literature by means of this dedication—since you have more need of a bridle than of spurs—but so that my greatest goodwill toward you might become known to everyone through this letter, on account of your divine genius, your multifaceted learning, and your knowledge of many languages. 

For you, not yet having reached your twenty-fourth year, are most learned in the humanistic studies of both languages <note>referring to Latin and Greek</note>; nor are you less skilled in Hebrew; and now you apply yourself to the study of both Chaldean <note>A term often used in this period to refer to Aramaic.</note> and Arabic with such zeal that men will shortly marvel at you for having five hearts. For by this logic, you already possess three, as the great Ennius <note>The early Roman poet Ennius famously said he had "three hearts" because he could speak Greek, Oscan, and Latin.</note> once said of himself. Furthermore, you pronounce <unclear>Greek</unclear> words with such fluency of tongue, and you <unclear>breathe life into</unclear> Hebrew with such fitness and ease, as if you were born and raised in the middle of Athens, or in the middle of the <unclear>land</unclear> of the Israelites at the time when they still stood.

<summary>In this dedication, the printer Aldus Manutius defends his practice of dedicating classical works to his friends and praises the young prodigy Girolamo Aleandro for his mastery of five languages.</summary>
<keywords>Aldus Manutius, Girolamo Aleandro, dedication, Neacademia, Ennius, linguistic mastery, printing history, Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication from Aldus Manutius to the scholar Girolamo Aleandro, following the discussion of Aleandro’s mastery of Hebrew and Aramaic. There is a physical stain on the bottom right of the original page, making the final words difficult to read.</meta>

...you might achieve. What shall I say of our own language, that is, Latin? In this you so excel that in the "equestrian" style <note>Latin: *equestri oratione*. A metaphor for poetry or elevated verse, contrasted with the "pedestrian" style of prose.</note> you have already completed great and learned books of lyrics, miscellaneous poems <note>original: *sylvarum*, referring to occasional or "forest-like" spontaneous poetry</note>, epigrams, and every kind of iambic verse. In the "pedestrian" style <note>Latin: *pedestri*, meaning prose</note>, you have finished letters, orations, dialogues, and many other works with a fortunate style. Whether all these are worthy of the approval of every most learned person, those into whose hands they will soon come shall judge. 

I omit mention of your knowledge of Music and the Mathematical arts, which you possess. I omit your study of all the liberal disciplines and of the universal "circle of education" <note>original Greek: *ἐγκυκλοπαιδείας* (enkyklopaideias), the root of the English word "encyclopedia," referring to a well-rounded education in the arts and sciences</note> as the Greeks call it. To this study you now devote your efforts day and night with indissoluble love and care at Padua <note>Latin: *Patavij*</note>, together with Maffeo Leone, a Venetian patrician and a young man of excellent genius who is most studious of refined literature.

But what is most worthy of praise of all: you are most distinguished in character, you are most Christian, nor do you think you should imitate certain most frivolous men. These men, so that they might seem to possess an excellent and overly delicate genius, as if scorning the common path of good men, have barely "sniffed" at the doctrines—if I may put it that way—before they turn out to be unfaithful, and as a consequence, most vicious. 

Since, therefore, I see that these qualities have met in no other man of our time, I have rightly dedicated the prince of poets <note>Referring to Homer</note> and the fountain of all learning to you—a most ingenious poet yourself and equally most studious of all learning. And since I see that Maffeo Leone himself, your Maecenas <note>A traditional term for a wealthy patron of the arts, named after the Roman advisor to Augustus</note>, is never lacking to you—and it is a marvel that he is so liberal in these stingy times—nevertheless, I want you to be able to promised yourself everything from me as well, most constantly. Therefore, I <unclear>would wish</unclear> you to be persuaded that I am one to whom, on account of your great virtues and your most holy character, you are as dear as you were to my father. F<unclear>arewell</unclear>.

<summary>Aldus Manutius concludes his dedication to Girolamo Aleandro, praising his mastery of Latin prose and poetry, his moral character, and his studies in Padua alongside his patron Maffeo Leone.</summary>
<keywords>Aldus Manutius, Girolamo Aleandro, Latin poetry, prose, Maffeo Leone, Padua, education, encyclopedia, patronage</keywords>

# ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST
# BOOK OF HOMER.

<margin>+</margin> Chryses, the priest of Apollo, arrives at the naval station <note>original: ναύσταθμον (naustathmon), the Greek camp where the ships were beached during the siege of Troy</note> of the Greeks, wishing to ransom his daughter, Chryseis. Not receiving her, however, but instead being driven away with insults by Agamemnon, he prayed to Apollo against the Greeks. A plague having occurred and many, as is likely, being destroyed, Achilles summoned an assembly. After Calchas clarified the true cause and Achilles ordered that they appease the god, Agamemnon became enraged; he quarreled with Achilles and snatched away his "prize of honor" <note>term: γέρας (geras), a specific type of gift or woman awarded to a hero to represent his social status and bravery</note>, Briseis. Because of this, Achilles is angry with the Greeks. Thetis, persuaded by her son, ascended to Olympus and requested of Zeus that he make the Trojans more powerful than the Greeks. Hera, having learned of this, quarreled with Zeus until Hephaestus reconciled them by serving wine in a golden cup. Having feasted for the remainder of the day, they turned to sleep.

<summary>This page provides a concise prose summary (Hypothesis) of the plot of the first book of the Iliad, detailing the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon and the subsequent divine intervention.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Iliad, Book 1, Achilles, Agamemnon, Chryses, Apollo, Thetis, Zeus, Hera, Hephaestus, Briseis, Trojan War, Argument</keywords>

<meta>catchword: -shall</meta>

But this did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus; 
instead, he dismissed the priest harshly and laid a heavy command upon him:
<margin>Threat</margin> “Old man, let me not find you near the hollow ships,
either lingering now or coming back here later,
<margin>Tyrannical speech</margin> lest the staff and the wreath of the god fail to protect you! 
As for the girl, I will not set her free. Before that, old age shall come upon her 
in our house in Argos <note>The kingdom of Agamemnon in Greece.</note>, far from her native land,
working at the loom and sharing my bed. 
But go! Do not provoke me, if you wish to return home in safety.”
So he spoke. The old man was afraid and obeyed his word. 
<margin>With a gesture</margin> He went in silence along the shore of the loud-roaring sea. 
Then, when he had gone far away, the old man prayed 
earnestly to King Apollo, whom fair-haired Leto bore:
<margin>Prayer</margin> “Hear me, Lord of the Silver Bow, you who protect Chryse
and sacred Cilla, and who rule mightily over Tenedos! 
Smintheus <note>A title for Apollo often translated as "Mouse-god," referring to his power to both cause and cure plague.</note>, if ever I roofed a temple to please you, 
or if ever I burned for you fat thigh-pieces 
of bulls or goats, grant me this wish: 
<margin>The Request</margin> May the Greeks <note>original: "Danaoi" (Danaans), one of Homer's names for the Greeks.</note> pay for my tears with your arrows!”
<margin>The priest’s just prayer</margin> So he spoke in prayer, and Phoebus Apollo heard him. 
<margin>Arrival of the God</margin> He came down from the peaks of Olympus, furious in his heart, 
carrying his bow on his shoulders and his hooded quiver. 
The arrows clashed on the shoulders of the angry god 
as he moved; and he came like the night. 
He sat down away from the ships and let fly an arrow; 
terrible was the twang of the silver bow. 
First he attacked the mules and the swift dogs, 
<margin>Often and together; many [arrows] were a great evil to men <note>original: "πολλάκι καὶ ξύν. πολλὰ πολὺ κακὸν ἀνθρωπ ἔσαν."</note></margin> but then he aimed his piercing shafts at the men themselves 
<margin>Sign of a great disaster</margin> and struck. Constantly, the funeral pyres of the dead burned thick. 
For nine days the god’s arrows ranged through the army.

“Oh you weaklings, shameful cowards, *Achaean women, no longer Achaean men,* <note>Original: *achaïdes ouk et' achaioi* — A biting insult questioning the masculinity and bravery of the soldiers.</note>

<margin>A stern rebuke</margin>
“*Thersites, reckless in speech, though you are a clear-voiced orator,*

hurling insults at them, while you watch for the return home.
We do not yet know clearly how these things will turn out,
whether we sons of the <term>Achaeans</term> <note>One of the primary names Homer uses for the Greeks.</note> shall return well or ill.

### ILIAD BOOK 2: Thoas, leader of the Aetolians <note>original: "ΙΛΙΑΔΟΣ· Β΄. Thoas dux aetolorum"</note>

Thoas, son of Andraemon, led the Aetolians,
who inhabited Pleuron, Olenos, and Pylene,
along with coastal Chalcis and rocky Calydon.
For the sons of great-hearted Oeneus were no longer living,
nor was the king himself still alive; and fair-haired Meleager <note>Meleager was a famous hero of the Calydonian Boar hunt; his death left the throne to the line of his father's brother.</note> was dead.
To Thoas, then, was entrusted the rule over all the Aetolians,
and forty black ships followed him.

<margin>Idomeneus</margin>
<margin>Cretans <note>original Latin: "Cretenses"</note></margin>
Idomeneus, famous for his spear, led the Cretans,
who held Knossos and walled Gortyn,
Lyktos and Miletos and chalky Lykastos,
Phaistos and Rhytion, well-inhabited cities,
and others who dwelt across hundred-citied Crete.
Of these, spear-famed Idomeneus was the leader,
along with Meriones, a peer of Enyalios <term>Enyalios: An ancient epithet for Ares, the god of war</term>, the slayer of men.
And eighty black ships followed them.

<margin>Rhodes Tlepolemus</margin>
Tlepolemus, the son of Heracles, both brave and tall,
led nine ships of the proud Rhodians from Rhodes.
They inhabited Rhodes, organized into three divisions:
Lindos, Ialysos, and chalky Cameirus.
Of these, spear-famed Tlepolemus was the leader,
whom Astyocheia bore to the might of Heracles,
whom he had brought from Ephyre, from the river Selleis,
after laying waste to many cities of Zeus-nurtured warriors.
But when Tlepolemus had grown up in the well-built palace,
he immediately slew his father’s beloved maternal uncle,
Licymnius, a branch of Ares <term>Branch of Ares: A poetic way of describing a warrior of noble or divine descent</term>, who was already growing old.
He quickly built ships, and having gathered many people,
he went fleeing across the sea; for they had threatened him—
the other sons and grandsons of the might of Heracles.
But he came to Rhodes in his wandering, suffering woes.

The Trojans were holding their assembly at Priam's gates,

and let him lead them out, having set his own citizens in order."

So she spoke, and Hector did not at all ignore the goddess’s word;

# ILIAD, BOOK 3

## SUMMARY OF THE THIRD BOOK OF HOMER’S POEM

After Alexander <note>original Greek: "Lexandrou" (Alexandrou) — Alexander is the alternative name for Paris, the Trojan prince who sparked the war by taking Helen.</note> challenged Menelaus to a single combat to settle the entire conflict, oaths were made on the condition that the victor would take Helen and her possessions. When Alexander was defeated, Aphrodite snatched him away; and leading him to his own bedchamber, she summoned Helen from the wall. They then spoke with one another and went to sleep.

1. He varies the portraits of the leaders and provides a comparison of the virtues of each. <note>This refers to the "Teichoscopia" or "view from the wall," where Helen identifies the Greek heroes for King Priam.</note>
2. A rich and abundant style of oratory in Ulysses <note>The Roman name for Odysseus.</note>, but a brief and Laconic <note>original Latin: "Laconismum" — referring to the famously pithy and direct speech style of the Spartans (Laconians).</note> style in Menelaus.
3. The elders of the city of Troy possess a <insert>sweet</insert> eloquence, almost like that of a swan. <note>In the poem, Homer compares the voices of the Trojan elders to the sound of cicadas, though this commentator uses the swan metaphor for their "swan song" as old men.</note> Eloquence full of Vulcan <note>original Latin: "Vulcani plena" — likely meaning fiery, intense, or forged with divine skill like the works of the blacksmith god Vulcan.</note>.
4. Having imitated first how his own dispute comes to be: the fathers in the <unclear>throat</unclear> <note>original Latin: "pharingi" — possibly a reference to the voice or a specific anatomical metaphor for speech.</note>; Virgil at the end of the *Aeneid* <note>The commentator notes how Virgil's Roman epic mimics this duel in the final fight between Aeneas and Turnus.</note>, but others [describe] the downfall.

# HOMER’S
## ILIAD · BOOK 4 · HOMER’S
## RHAPSODY <note>A "rhapsody" refers to a book or a distinct section of an epic poem, traditionally recited by a professional performer known as a rhapsode.</note>

<margin>5</margin> It was the will of the gods that Ilium <note>Another name for the city of Troy.</note> should be captured; for this reason, the goddess Athena arranged for Menelaus to be shot with an arrow by Pandarus. In this way, the sacred oaths <note>The truce established in the previous book to decide the war by a single duel.</note> were violated. Machaon <note>The physician of the Greek army and son of the god of medicine, Asclepius.</note> then heals Menelaus, while Agamemnon, moving through the ranks, rouses the army for war. Once the battle began, many men from both sides were slain.

<insert>
Human affairs are attributed to the Gods <note>original Latin: "Humanae res referre ad Deos"</note> as Lucian notes regarding Thucydides, Book 1 <note>original Latin: "ut Luc: in Thuc: 1." This likely refers to a scholarly commentary comparing how historians and poets treat divine intervention.</note>.

The Gods conspire here, just as the Triumvirs <note>The "Triumvirate" refers to the political alliances of three powerful men in ancient Rome, such as Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus. The annotator sees the gods' secret planning as a form of cynical political maneuvering.</note> did at Rome. <note>original Latin: "Conspirant hic Dij, ut apud Rom: Triumviri"</note>

# SUMMARY OF THE FIFTH BOOK OF HOMER’S ILIAD

Diomedes, with the goddess Athena assisting him, performs great feats of valor <note>The Greek term is 'aristeia,' denoting a hero’s peak moment of excellence on the battlefield</note>, and slays many of the enemy. He even wounds the goddess Aphrodite in the hand, and the god Ares in the flank <note>original: "keneonos" — the soft part of the body or the groin</note>. When Aeneas is struck by Diomedes with a stone, Apollo rescues him from the field. Tlepolemus is killed by Sarpedon, and Zeus rebukes Ares for his interference; Ares is subsequently healed by Paeon <note>original: "Paieon" — the physician of the Olympian gods</note>, the doctor of the gods.

<insert>
Virgil <note>The author of this manuscript includes a parallel passage from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (10.270-275), comparing the hero's shining armor to a dangerous star</note>:
The peak of his helmet blazes on his head and a flame pours from the crests at the top, and the golden shield-boss vomits forth vast fires—not unlike when, in the clear night, blood-red comets glow mournfully, or the burning heat of Sirius <note>The "Dog Star," which ancient Greeks and Romans believed brought heatwaves and pestilence</note>. That star rises, bringing thirst and diseases to weary mortals, and saddens the sky with its ill-omened light.
</insert>

<margin>Diomedes' Prayer to Pallas Athena</margin>
Then Diomedes, good at the war-cry, prayed:
"Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, unwearied one! 
If ever with kindly thought you stood by my father 
in the heat of battle, now again show me your love, Athena.
Grant that I may slay this man, and come within spear-cast of him 
who struck me first and now boasts, saying I shall 
not long look upon the bright light of the sun."

so did strong Diomedes, in his fury, mingle with the Trojans.

But I did not listen—though it would have been much better—sparing my horses so that they might not lack for fodder in a crowded city, accustomed as they are to eating their fill."

And the goddesses returned again to the house of great Zeus—Argive Hera and Athena of Alalcomene <note>An epithet for Athena, likely referring to a town where she was worshipped or meaning "The Protectress."</note>—having stopped man-destroying Ares from his slaughter of men.

With the gods having withdrawn from the battle, the Greeks slay many of the Trojans. Upon the advice of Helenos <note>A son of King Priam who served as a seer for the Trojan side.</note>, Hector goes up into the city and commands his mother Hecuba to pray to Athena and to promise her a sacrifice of twelve heifers, so that the goddess might drive Diomedes <note>The Greek hero who dominated the previous book of the poem.</note> away from the battle. Hector, after speaking with his mother Hecuba and his wife Andromache, goes out to the war with his brother Alexander <note>The prince also known as Paris, whose abduction of Helen sparked the war.</note>.

### ARGUMENT OF THE SEVENTH BOOK <note>original: "Η." (Eta). In the Greek numeral system, this letter represents the number 7.</note> OF HOMER’S POEM.

->K<- <note>This "K" is a signature mark, used by early printers to keep the large sheets of paper in the correct order for binding.</note>

Hector, having gone down into battle with his brother Alexander <note>Alexander is another name for Paris.</note>, brought aid to the Trojans who were already growing weary. On the advice of his brother Helenus, who was a seer, Hector himself issued a challenge to see which of the Greeks might wish to engage him in single combat. When many volunteered, Ajax the son of Telamon was chosen by lot and stood against him. While they were fighting, heralds called them to a stop, and night dissolved the battle. The two then gave gifts to one another. After the heroes had sent heralds to negotiate for the recovery of the dead, the same burial rites were performed by both armies. The Greeks then constructed a common grave for their many fallen and built a wall to protect their <term>naval camp</term> <note>original: "ναυστάθμῳ" (naustathmō). This refers to the place where the Greek ships were beached and their shelters were built.</note>, an act which made the god Poseidon indignant. Throughout the night, Zeus showed them unfavorable signs of things to come.

“Ajax, Zeus-born, son of Telamon, leader of the people,
do not try to test me as if I were some feeble boy,
or a woman who knows nothing of the works of war.
For I myself well know both battles and the slaying of men.
I know how to shift my shield of seasoned ox-hide to the right,
and I know how to shift it to the left; this is what it means to be a hardy warrior.
I know how to charge into the din of swift horses,
and I know how to dance the dance of the god of war <note>The Greek "melpesthai arei" literally means to "dance for Ares," suggesting that high-stakes combat has its own lethal rhythm or choreography.</note> in close-quarters fighting.

He spoke, and brandishing his long-shadowed spear, he hurled it,
and he struck Ajax’s dread shield of seven-layered ox-hide,
hitting the outermost bronze, which was the eighth layer upon it.
The unwearying bronze went cleaving through six folds,
but it was stayed in the seventh hide. Then, in his turn,
Zeus-born Ajax hurled his long-shadowed spear,
and he struck the shield of the son of Priam <note>Hector.</note>, which was perfectly round.
Through the shining shield the mighty spear passed,
and it was driven through the elaborately worked breastplate;
straight through, beside the flank, the spear tore the tunic.
But Hector leaned aside and escaped black death.

### SUMMARY OF THE EIGHTH BOOK OF HOMER’S ILIAD.
<note>original Greek: "ΥΠΟΘΕΣΙΣ ΤΗΣ Θ. ΟΜΗΡΟΥ ΡΑΨΩΔΙΑΣ." The letter Theta (Θ) signifies the eighth book of the epic. A "Hypothesis" in this context is a scholarly summary of the plot.</note>

8. Zeus, having forbidden the other gods from helping either of the two armies, descends to Mount Ida; and though the Greeks were previously fighting on equal terms, he now makes them inferior to the Trojans. When Hera and Athena set out to provide aid to the Greeks, Iris stops them at the command of Zeus. When evening fell, Hector delivered a speech to the people on the plain, so that they might camp there and keep fires burning throughout the whole night.

<margin>A Lament</margin>
“Shall we no longer care for the dying Danaans <note>The Greeks</note>, even at this final hour? They are perishing, fulfilling a miserable fate at the hands of one man’s onset. He rages beyond endurance—Hector, son of Priam—and has already wrought many evils.”

<margin>A Curse</margin>
“Indeed, let this man lose his strength and his life, falling at the hands of the Argives <note>The Greeks</note> in his own native land.
<margin>A Transition</margin>
But my father <note>Zeus</note> rages with a wicked mind; he is cruel, a constant sinner, and a thwarter of my purposes.
<margin>A Lament</margin>
He remembers none of the many times I saved his son <note>The hero Heracles</note> when he was worn down by the labors imposed by Eurystheus.
<margin>Amplification through frustration: a comparison of favors granted.</margin>
Truly, he would weep toward heaven, and Zeus would send me down from the skies to help him. If I had known how this would end—with my father now favoring the Trojans—back when Heracles was sent to the house of Hades the Gate-Fastener to bring the hound of hateful Hades <note>Cerberus</note> out of Erebus, he would never have escaped the steep-falling waters of the Styx <note>The river of the underworld</note>.
But now Zeus hates me and fulfills the wishes of Thetis, who kissed his knees and took his beard in her hand, begging him to honor Achilles, the sacker of cities. Yet the time will come when he calls me his 'dear grey-eyed daughter' once more. But come, prepare our single-hoofed horses, while I enter the palace of aegis-bearing Zeus to arm myself in armor for war. I wish to see if Hector of the glancing helmet, son of Priam, will rejoice when the two of us appear upon the bridges of war <note>The open spaces of the battlefield</note>. Surely many a Trojan will also sate the dogs and birds with his fat and flesh, falling dead beside the ships of the Achaeans.”
So she spoke, and the white-armed goddess Hera did not disobey. She went to prepare the horses with the golden headbands.

-># THE ILIAD.<-

“Where are you two rushing? Why does the **heart rage in your breasts?** The son of Cronus <note>Zeus, the king of the gods</note> does not allow you to give aid to the Greeks. For the son of Cronus threatened thus, and he will surely fulfill it: he will cripple your swift horses under the chariot, <margin>The goddesses are recalled</margin> hurl you yourselves from the chariot-seat, and smash the chariot to pieces. Not even in ten circling years will you be healed of the wounds that his lightning bolt shall strike you; so that you, bright-eyed goddess <note>Athena</note>, may know what it means when you fight against your own father. Against Hera he is not so much indignant or angry, for she is always accustomed **to thwart whatever he intends.** **But you, most fearless and shameless dog, if indeed you truly** dare to raise your giant spear against Zeus.”

Having spoken thus, swift-footed Iris departed; but Hera spoke a word to Athena: “Alas, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, I no longer wish for the two of us to fight against Zeus for the sake of mortals. <margin>Juno and Pallas yield</margin> Let one of them perish and **let another live,** whoever it may be; and let Zeus, **musing on his own designs in his heart,** live and pass judgment on both the Greeks and the Trojans, as is fitting.”

So she spoke, and turned back her solid-hoofed horses. The Hours <note>The *Horae*, goddesses who guarded the gates of heaven</note> unyoked the fair-maned horses for them, tied them to their immortal mangers, and leaned the chariot against the shimmering inner walls. The goddesses themselves sat upon golden couches among the other gods, their hearts deeply troubled.

<margin>Jupiter returns to Heaven from Ida</margin> Then father Zeus drove his well-wheeled chariot and horses from Mount Ida to Olympus, and arrived at the assembly of the gods. For him, the illustrious Earth-shaker <note>Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes</note> unyoked the horses, placed the chariot upon its stand, and spread a linen cloth over it. And Zeus himself, the wide-seeing, sat upon his golden throne...

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE NINTH BOOK <note>original: "I"</note> OF HOMER

When Agamemnon advised the Greeks to flee, Diomedes and Nestor stood up and expressed the opposite opinion. At Nestor's advice, envoys were sent to Achilles; though they pleaded with him, Achilles spoke against them. They, in turn, reported back; and after this, they turned to sleep.

# THE SUMMARY OF HOMER'S
# TENTH BOOK.

<margin>10</margin> Agamemnon, being unable to sleep, rouses the best of the Greeks, both he himself and Menelaus. Having taken counsel at the trench <note>A defensive ditch dug by the Greeks to protect their camp</note>, they send scouts to the camp of the Trojans: Odysseus and Diomedes. These two, meeting a man named Dolon on the way, kill him. Having learned from him about a certain Rhesus and that Thracians are present, they go to where they had encamped and murder them by stealth. Then, driving the horses away, they return to the ship-camp.

He found him putting his fine armor around his shoulders
by the stern of his ship; and his arrival was welcome to him.

# ILIAD BOOK 10

<insert>Rhesus falls</insert>

As a lion comes upon an unprotected flock of goats or sheep with evil intent, so did the son of Tydeus <note>Diomedes, one of the greatest Greek warriors</note> fall upon the Thracian men until he had slain twelve. Meanwhile, resourceful Odysseus, whenever the son of Tydeus stood over a man and struck him with his sword, would seize the body from behind by the foot and drag it out of the way. He did this with a plan in his mind: so that the beautiful-maned horses might pass through easily and not be frightened in their hearts by treading on the dead, for they were not yet accustomed to corpses.

But when the son of Tydeus reached the King <note>Rhesus, the Thracian leader</note>, he took from him his honey-sweet life—the thirteenth victim—as he lay gasping. For an evil dream stood over his head that night, sent by the grandson of Oineus <note>Diomedes himself, appearing like a nightmare</note> through the counsel of Athena.

During this time, the enduring Odysseus untied the solid-hoofed horses and bound them together with leather reins. He began to drive them out of the throng, striking them with his bow, because he had not thought to take the shining whip from the ornate chariot-seat.

<margin>whistling <note>original Latin: "sibilatus"</note></margin>
Then he whistled, signaling to the noble Diomedes. But Diomedes remained behind, pondering what more daring deed he might do: whether he should seize the chariot where the ornate armor lay and pull it out by the pole, or lift it up and carry it away, <margin>Consultation in a sudden crisis <note>original Latin: "Consultatio in re subitâ"</note></margin> or whether he should take the lives of even more Thracians.

<margin>Rhesus [slain] by Pallas [Athena] <note>original Latin: "Rhesus a pallade"</note></margin>
While he was turning these thoughts over in his mind, Athena stood near and spoke to the noble Diomedes: "Think now of your return to the hollow ships, son of great-hearted Tydeus, lest you arrive there in flight, or lest some other god rouses the Trojans against you."

So she spoke, and he recognized the voice of the goddess. Quickly he mounted the horses; Odysseus struck them with his bow, and they sped toward the swift ships of the Achaeans. But Apollo, God of the Silver Bow, kept no blind watch.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE ELEVENTH BOOK <note>Book Lambda</note> OF HOMER’S POEM

Agamemnon, having armed himself and having seen the other Greeks <note>The text uses "Hellenes," the name the Greeks used for themselves</note> fully armed, leads them out to war. Hector, at the command of Zeus, withdraws from the fighting until Agamemnon is driven back to the naval camp <note>the fortified area where the Greek ships were beached</note>. Following this, when the Trojans have surrounded Odysseus, he defends himself against them, with Ajax and Menelaus coming to his aid. Nevertheless, the finest of the Greeks are wounded: Agamemnon by Coön; Odysseus by Socus; while Diomedes, Eurypylus, and Machaon are struck by the arrows of Alexander <note>Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen started the war</note>. Achilles, having seen Machaon returning with Nestor, sends Patroclus to learn who the wounded man was. After arriving and finding it was Machaon, Patroclus is urged by Nestor to either persuade Achilles to join the Greeks in battle, or at least to go into the fight himself wearing Achilles' own panoply <term>panoply: a complete suit of armor</term>. <gloss>Patroclus</gloss> On his way back, he encounters Eurypylus and, bringing him to the ships, tends to his wounds.

Let us also direct our horses and chariot there, where cavalry and infantry are most of all engaging in evil strife and slaughtering one another, and where the unquenchable war-cry has arisen."

### THE ILIAD, BOOK 11 <note>The header "Σ" usually refers to Book 18, but the text here is clearly from Book 11, lines 714–744.</note>

A messenger came running from Olympus <note>the goddess Athena</note> to tell us to arm ourselves by night; she did not gather an unwilling people in Pylos, but those who were very eager to fight. Yet Neleus <note>Nestor’s father</note> would not let me arm myself; he hid away my horses, for he said I did not yet understand the works of war. But even so, I was preeminent among our horsemen, even though I was on foot; for that is how Athena led the conflict.

There is a river called Minyeius that empties into the sea near Thryoessa; there we waited for the divine Dawn, we the horsemen of the Pylians, while the throngs of foot soldiers flowed in after us. From there, in full haste and armored in our gear, we reached the sacred stream of Alpheios at midday. There we offered fine sacrifices to almighty Zeus: a bull to Alpheios, a bull to Poseidon, but to grey-eyed Athena, a heifer from the herd. Then we took our meal throughout the camp in our divisions and lay down to sleep, each in our armor, along the streams of the river. 

Meanwhile, the great-hearted Epeians were surrounding the city, eager to sack it; but before they could, a great work of the War-god <note>original: "Arēs"</note> appeared to them.

At once he spoke winged words to the son of Oileus <note>Ajax the Lesser, the swifter but smaller of the two heroes named Ajax</note>: "Ajax, you and the mighty Lycomedes stay here and urge the Danaans <note>The Greeks</note> to fight with all their might. <margin>Ajax brings help to Menestheus</margin>
Having spoken thus, Telamonian Ajax departed, and Teucer his brother, born of the same father, went with him; and with them Pandion **carried the curved bows**. When they reached the tower of great-hearted Menestheus, they went inside the wall and found the men hard-pressed. The mighty leaders and rulers of the Lycians were mounting the battlements like a dark whirlwind. They clashed in battle face to face, and the war-cry rose up.

<margin>The assault and slaughter</margin>
Telamonian Ajax was the first to kill a man, the great-hearted Epicles, a companion of Sarpedon, striking him with a jagged stone that lay inside the wall. It lay there, huge, by the battlement at the very top; not even a man in the prime of youth, such as mortals are now <note>A common Homeric trope: the heroes of the past were far stronger than the people of the poet's own day</note>, could easily hold it in both hands. 

<margin>A huge stone</margin>
But Ajax lifted it high and threw it. He <margin>shattered</margin> the four-crested helmet and crushed the bones of the head all at once; Epicles fell like a diver from the high tower, and his spirit left his bones. Then Teucer struck Glaucus, the powerful son of Hippolochus, with an arrow as he was rushing the high wall.

### SUMMARY OF THE 13TH BOOK OF HOMER’S ILIAD <note>The "Hypothesis" was a common feature in ancient and medieval manuscripts, providing a brief plot summary before the start of a new section.</note>

of them <gloss>the Trojans</gloss> are also killed. Deiphobus and Helenos 
are wounded. Gathering his subjects together, Hector leads them 
against the enemy; and there is great slaughter on both sides.

<margin>Menelaus rebukes the Trojans <note>original Latin: "Menelaus increpat Troian[os]"</note></margin>
"So shall you leave the ships of the fast-horsed Danaans <note>another name for the Greeks</note>, you cowardly Trojans, never sated with the cry of battle. You have not lacked for other outrages and shameful deeds—the harms you did to me, you vile dogs. Nor did you fear in your hearts the heavy wrath of thundering Zeus, the <term>Guest-God</term><note>The god who protects the sacred laws of hospitality (Xenia), which Paris broke by stealing Helen from her host, Menelaus.</note>, who shall one day destroy your towering city. You carried off my wedded wife and many of my possessions, stealing them away wantonly, even though you had been treated with kindness by her. Now, you even hunger to cast destructive fire upon our sea-faring ships and to slaughter the Achaean heroes. But you shall be held back, however eager you are for war! Father Zeus, they say that you surpass all others in wisdom, both men and gods, and yet all these things come from you. How you favor these insolent men—these Trojans, whose might is always lawless, and who can never have their fill of the din of equal war."

<margin>There is a satiety of all things <note>original Latin: "Omnium rerum satietas est"</note></margin>
**"There is a satiety of all things: of sleep, and of love,**
**and of sweet song, and the noble dance.**
Of these things, surely, a man would rather satisfy his desire than of war; but the Trojans are insatiable in battle."
So speaking, the noble Menelaus stripped the blood-stained armor from the body and gave it to his companions; then he himself turned back and rejoined the front ranks of the fighters. There, Harpalion, the son of King Pylaemenes, leapt upon him. He had followed his dear father to war at Troy, but he was never to return to his native land. He then struck the middle of the son of Atreus's <note>Menelaus's</note> shield with his spear from close at hand, but he could not drive the bronze point all the way through. He shrank back into the crowd of his companions to avoid death, glancing warily in every direction, lest someone should graze his flesh with bronze.

<margin>Harpalion, son of Pylaemenes, falls <note>original Latin: "Harpalion Pylaemenis filius cadit"</note></margin>
But as he was retreating, <term>Meriones</term><note>A prominent Greek commander from Crete.</note> let fly a bronze-tipped arrow at him. He hit him in the right buttock, and the arrow passed straight through, under the bone, and into the bladder.

### THE ARGUMENT OF THE 16TH BOOK OF HOMER’S ILIAD
<note>An "Argument" (Greek: Hypothesis) is a traditional summary provided by ancient and medieval scholars to help readers follow the plot of each book.</note>

At the request of Patroclus, Achilles allows him to take up his own **armor** and to lead the **Myrmidons** <note>The elite group of warriors led by Achilles</note> out to war. When these set out, they turned the Trojans to flight. Patroclus kills Sarpedon, the son of Zeus, after Sarpedon had killed Pedasos, the <term>trace-horse</term> <note>An extra horse harnessed alongside the main pair in a chariot</note> of Achilles. Then Hector kills Patroclus, after Patroclus had first been struck by Euphorbus and the god Apollo, who had stripped away his armor.

As ravenous wolves fall upon lambs or kids, snatching them from the flocks when they have been scattered across the mountains by a shepherd’s lack of care; the wolves, seeing them, immediately seize the weak-hearted creatures. So the Danaans <note>original: "danaoi" — one of Homer's names for the Greeks.</note> fell upon the Trojans; and the Trojans thought only of disastrous flight, forgetting their furious valor.

Great Ajax <note>The son of Telamon, the strongest of the Greek warriors after Achilles.</note> was forever aiming at Hector of the bronze helmet, eager to strike him with a javelin. But Hector, with his expertise in war, covered his broad shoulders with his bull-hide shield, <margin>lookout</margin> watching the whirring of the arrows and the thud of the spears. He truly recognized that the tide of victory in battle was turning; yet even so, he remained and sought to save his loyal companions.

<margin>Comparison</margin> As when a cloud comes from Olympus into the heavens, out of the divine air, when Zeus stretches forth a whirlwind—so the clamor and the flight of the Trojans came from the ships. They did not cross the trench <note>The defensive ditch the Greeks dug to protect their camp and ships.</note> back toward the city in good order. His swift-footed horses carried Hector away with his armor, but he left behind the Trojan people, whom the dug trench held back against their will. Many swift, chariot-pulling horses snapped their poles at the front and left the chariots of their masters behind.

But Patroclus followed, calling out harshly to the Greeks, with evil intent for the Trojans. They, with clamor and flight, filled all the paths, for they were scattered. High up, a whirlwind of dust <note>original: "aella"</note> spread under the clouds, and the solid-hoofed horses were stretched to their limit heading back toward the city, away from the ships and the huts.

<margin>The deeds of Patroclus</margin> Wherever Patroclus saw the crowd in the greatest confusion, there he drove, shouting a war-cry. Men fell headlong from their chariots beneath his axles, and the cars were overturned with a crash. Straight across the trench leaped those swift horses—immortal ones, which the gods gave as glorious gifts to Peleus <note>Achilles' father; these horses are Xanthus and Balius, who were divine and could speak.</note>—as they strained forward. Patroclus’ heart urged him against Hector, for he was eager to strike him, but Hector’s swift horses carried him away.

<margin>The prayer of Glaucus <note>original: "Precatio glaucj"</note></margin>

Glaucus knew this in his mind and rejoiced because the great god had quickly heard his prayer. First, he went everywhere among the Lycians, urging their leaders to fight for the body of Sarpedon.

## SUMMARY OF THE 17TH BOOK 
## OF HOMER.

Concerning the body of **Patroclus**, a mighty battle is joined, during which **Euphorbus** is slain by **Menelaus**. **Hector** puts on the armor of **Achilles** and they <note>the Trojans</note> withstand the **Greeks**. Those around **Menelaus** dispatch **Antilochus** to **Achilles** to report the death of **Patroclus**. Ducking under and lifting the body, they carry it on their shoulders; the two **Ajaxes** <note>Ajax the Greater and Ajax the Lesser</note> fight in the front lines and keep the enemies at bay.

# THE ILIAD <note>original: "ΙΛΙΑΔΟΣ"</note>

They stood locked shield-to-shield; for they were fenced in on all sides as they stood around **Patroclus**, holding their spears out before them. **Ajax** ranged among them all, giving many orders; he commanded that no man should fall back from the corpse, nor should any Greek fight out in front of the others, but rather they should stand firm around the body and fight hand-to-hand.

Such were the orders of giant **Ajax**. The earth was soaked with purple blood; the dead fell thick and fast—the corpses of Trojans and their brave allies, and of the Danaans <note>The Greeks</note> too. For they did not fight without shedding blood, though far fewer of the Greeks perished; they always remembered to shield one another in the throng from the bitter toil <term>toil: a common Homeric metaphor for the exhausting work of battle</term> of war.

So they fought like a blazing fire. You would not have said that either the sun or moon were still safe in the heavens, for they were shrouded in a mist of battle—all those champions who stood around the fallen **son of Menoetius** <note>Patroclus</note>. 

Meanwhile, the other Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans fought at their ease under a clear sky; the sharp light of the sun spread over them, and no cloud appeared over <gloss>the whole</gloss> <note>original Latin gloss: "integrae"</note> earth or over <gloss>the mountains</gloss> <note>original Latin gloss: "montium"</note>. These men fought with pauses, avoiding each other's painful missiles and standing far apart. 

But those in the center suffered agony from the mist and the war, worn down by the pitiless bronze—all those who were the best among them. # THE ILIAD

And for those fighting all day, a great and grueling conflict arose. With unceasing labor and sweat, the knees, shanks, and feet of every man, and their hands and eyes, were splattered with gore as they fought over the noble attendant of the swift-footed **grandson of Aeacus** <note>Patroclus, the squire and companion of Achilles</note>.

<margin>A Comparison</margin>
As when a man gives the hide of a great bull to his people to stretch, once it is soaked in fat; they take it and stand apart in a circle to pull it. Immediately the moisture leaves the skin and the fat sinks in as many hands tug, until the whole hide is stretched taut in every direction.

<margin>The Application</margin>
In just such a way, both sides tugged the corpse back and forth in a narrow space. Their hearts were filled with hope: the **Trojans** hoped to drag him to **Ilium** <note>Troy</note>, but the **Achaeans** <note>the Greeks</note> to the hollow ships. Around him the wild struggle grew fierce; neither **Ares**, the stirrer of armies, nor **Athena** could have looked upon that sight and found fault, even if great anger had come upon them.

<margin>A bitter battle / The poet continues</margin>
Such was the terrible toil of men and horses that **Zeus** stretched over **Patroclus** on that day. Nor did noble **Achilles** yet know anything of **Patroclus's** death.

<margin>Returning to Achilles</margin>
For they were fighting far away from the swift ships, beneath the wall of the **Trojans**. Therefore, **Achilles** never imagined in his heart that his friend was dead; rather, he expected him to return alive after reaching the very gates. He did not think for a moment that they would sack the city without him, nor even with him. He had often heard this from his mother <note>The sea-nymph Thetis</note>, listening to her in private when she reported the will of great **Zeus** to him. 

But on this occasion, his mother had not told him of the terrible evil that had occurred—that his companion, by far the most beloved to him, had perished. 

Meanwhile, the others, holding their sharp spears, pressed on relentlessly around the corpse and slaughtered one another.

# SUMMARY OF THE 18TH BOOK—SIGMA—OF HOMER'S
# EPIC POEM

**Achilles**, having learned of **Patroclus's** death, mourns.
**Thetis** <note>Achilles' mother, a sea-nymph</note>, rising up from the sea,
comforts him; and she advises him to stay away from the war
until she can bring him armor from **Hephaestus** <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship</note>.
But at the command of **Hera** <note>Queen of the gods</note>, he goes unarmed to the trench;
he appears to the enemies, and they flee in terror;
and during the flight, many are destroyed. The **Myrmidons** <note>Achilles' elite soldiers</note>,
having rescued the body of **Patroclus**, wash it.
**Hephaestus** then prepares a full suit of armor for **Achilles**.

...the beautiful armor, a wonder to see, which Hector plundered and took away. The gods gave those glorious gifts to Peleus on the day they forced you into the marriage bed of a mortal man.
<margin>The Complaint of Achilles <note>original Latin: Achilles conquerimonia</note></margin> 
How I wish you had stayed there among the immortal sea-nymphs, and that Peleus had married a mortal woman instead! 
But now, you too must have infinite sorrow in your heart for your dying son—for you will never welcome him home again. My own spirit no longer drives me to live or remain among men, unless Hector is first struck down by my spear and loses his life, paying the price for despoiling Patroclus, son of Menoetius <note>Patroclus's father</note>.

Then Thetis answered him, shedding tears: 
"Then you will be short-lived, my child, based on what you say; for your own fate is ready immediately after Hector’s death."

Deeply moved, swift-footed Achilles replied: 
"Let me die this moment, since I was not there to protect my friend as he was being killed. He has perished far from his fatherland, and he needed me to be his protector against ruin. 
Now, since I will not return to my dear fatherland, and I did not become a light of safety for Patroclus or my other companions—many of whom have been struck down by noble Hector—I sit here by the ships, a useless burden on the earth. 
I, who am like no other of the bronze-clad Achaeans <note>A common name for the Greek forces</note> in war, even if others are better in the public assembly. 
<margin>Strife and Anger <note>original Latin: Contentio et Ira</note></margin> 
Would that strife might perish from among gods and men, and anger likewise, which goads even a wise man to bitterness. Anger is far sweeter than dripping honey, yet it grows like smoke in the chests of men—just as Agamemnon, lord of men, has now angered me. 
But we will let these things be, though it hurts us, for they are in the past.

They took their stand and fought a battle by the banks of the river;

They joined the throng and fought like living mortals,

The field grew black behind them and looked like plowed land,
even though it was made of gold; this was truly a wonder to behold.
Then he placed there a royal estate, where reapers

# SUMMARY OF THE 19TH BOOK OF HOMER'S ILIAD

Thetis brings the armor from Hephaestus to Achilles. The hero, having gathered the Greeks into an assembly, makes a formal renunciation of his anger <note>original: "aporrhēsin poieitai tēs mēnidos"—this is the pivotal moment where Achilles sets aside his "menis" or transformative rage against Agamemnon</note>. He then receives the gifts that Agamemnon had previously promised him. While the rest of the army takes their meal, Achilles remains fasting and prepares for battle by putting on his armor. He leads the army out to war; however, Xanthus, the second of his horses, prophesies his approaching death, for which Achilles rebukes him.

<margin>Bodies must be cared for before the fight <note>original Latin: "Corpora curanda esse ante pugna"</note></margin>
But command the Achaeans <note>The Greeks</note> to take their fill by the swift ships

For no man, all day long until the setting of the sun,

for even if his heart is eager for the battle,

has a bold heart within his breast, and his limbs

# SUMMARY OF THE 20TH CANTO OF HOMER

With Zeus looking down upon the scene, all the gods descend to offer their aid; on the side of the Greeks are Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hephaestus, and Hermes; while for the Trojans are Aphrodite and Apollo, as well as Artemis, Leto, Ares, and Scamander <note>The god of the local river in Troy</note>. Apollo <gloss>Phoebus</gloss> saves Aeneas when he stands against Achilles, covering him in a cloud to hide him; meanwhile, Achilles <margin>Against the long sentence <note>original Latin: "Contra sententia longin." This likely refers to a scholarly debate regarding the length or structure of this specific passage</note></margin> slays Dryops and Polydorus, the son of Priam. Hector, having stood against Achilles, flees when Apollo saves him; then Achilles drove the others as they fled toward the city.

## HYPOTHESIS OF THE 21ST BOOK <note>original: "Φ." The letter Phi represents the number 21 in the Greek counting system.</note> OF HOMER'S
## RHAPSODY

The Trojans having been divided into two parts, Achilles
pursues some toward the city and others into the Scamander River;
and he takes twelve young men alive as a penalty for Patroclus; 
he himself kills Lycaon, the son of Priam, and Asteropaeus;
then, when the river overflows and endangers him,
Hephaestus saves him, having set fire to the river and the
plain; after these things, a battle of the gods against one another occurs;
Apollo then hinders Achilles by likening himself to Agenor,
and by fleeing, he deceives him until the Trojans are saved within the city.
<note>The "Hypothesis" was a standard ancient or medieval summary provided by scholars to guide the reader through the plot of the upcoming chapter.</note>

### ->SUMMARY OF THE 22ND (X)<-
### ->BOOK OF HOMER<-

While the Trojans were shut inside the city, Hector alone remained outside to face Achilles. At first, he flees; but then he stands his ground after Athena persuades him, and he is killed. Achilles, having bound him to his chariot, drags him across the plain toward the naval station <note>the Greek camp at the ships</note>. Those within the city wail as they watch these things from behind the gates.

But what if I go out to face the noble Achilles

<margin>His own private thoughts <note>original Latin: "Propria solum"</note></margin>

There is no way now to whisper with him "from an oak tree or a rock" <note>An ancient Greek idiom referring to intimate or casual conversation, perhaps echoing old myths or folk sayings about the origins of humanity</note>,

# THE ILIAD

### X.

So he <note>Achilles</note> flew straight at him in his fury, and Hector fled beneath the Trojan wall, moving his swift knees. They raced past the lookout point and the wind-swept wild fig tree, always away from the wall along the wagon track. They reached the two fair-flowing springs, where the twin sources of the swirling Scamander <note>The principal river of the Trojan plain, which the gods call Xanthus</note> well up.

<margin>
A poetic description of the place and the wondrous spring <note>original Latin: "Color poetice... descriptio: loci, mirandi fontis"</note>
</margin>

One spring flows with warm water, and smoke rises from it as if from a blazing fire. But even in summer, the other flows out as cold as hail or freezing snow, or ice formed from water. There, near the springs, are wide and beautiful washing-troughs made of stone, where the wives and lovely daughters of the Trojans used to wash their shimmering clothes in the days of peace, before the sons of the Achaeans <note>The Greeks</note> arrived.

Past these they ran, one fleeing, one pursuing behind. **A noble man fled in front, but a far greater one chased him** with speed. For they were not striving for a sacrificial beast or a bull's hide—the usual prizes for the racing feet of men—but they ran for the life of horse-taming Hector.

<margin>
A comparison of the flight <note>original Latin: "Compar fuga"</note>
</margin>

As when prize-winning, solid-hooved horses wheel rapidly around the turning-posts, and a great prize lies before them—perhaps a tripod <note>A three-legged bronze cauldron, a common prize in ancient Greek games</note> or a woman—to honor a man who has died, so these two circled Priam’s city three times on their swift feet. And all the gods looked on.

Among them, the father of men and gods <note>Zeus</note> began to speak:

<margin>
A digression: a conversation among the gods before the final resolution of the plot, just as Virgil does in the 12th book of the Aeneid <note>original Latin: "parecbasu colloquiu deoru ante oecononiā catastrophe sic in Virgilius in 12 Aenei"</note>
</margin>

<margin>A lament <note>original Latin: "Querela"</note></margin>

"Oh, how sad! With my own eyes I see a man I love being chased around the wall. My heart grieves for Hector, who has burned many thighs of oxen for me as a sacrifice on the peaks of many-ridged Ida, and at other times on the highest point of the city. But now, noble Achilles pursues him on swift feet around the city of Priam."

# THE SUMMARY OF BOOK 23 (PSI) OF HOMER’S
## ILIAD

<margin>
Funeral
games
<note>original Latin: "Ludi funebres"</note>
</margin>
Achilles performs the customary rites for the dead for Patroclus <note>Achilles' closest companion, whose death prompted Achilles to return to battle.</note>; having raised a burial mound and sacrificed twelve Trojan youths over him, as well as dogs, horses, and other sacrificial animals. Then he also holds funeral games, in which Diomedes wins the chariot race, and Odysseus wins the footrace, while others win in other contests; and thus the assembly for the games is dissolved. <gloss>games <unclear>p q v</unclear> regarding this book <note>The Latin gloss "ludicra ad hanc" refers to the "games" described in this section of the poem.</note></gloss>

So he spoke, and they wailed in a body; and Achilles led them. # Communion even in death <note>original Latin: "Communio etiam in morte"</note>
## THE ILIAD <note>original Greek: "ILIADOS"</note>

<margin>I ask that my bones be laid together <note>original Latin: "Peto ut mea ossa coniuncta Componi"</note></margin>
"Do not lay my bones apart from yours, Achilles,
but together, just as we were raised in your house;
when Menoetius <note>Patroclus's father</note> brought me as a small child from Opoeis

foolishly and without intent, angered over a game of dice.
Then the knight Peleus <note>Achilles' father</note> received me into his halls,
reared me with kindness, and named me your squire.

<gloss>This marks the spirit of the one responding <note>original Latin: "Animum respondentis signat"</note></gloss>

embrace each other and take our fill of wretched mourning."
So saying, he reached out with his own hands
but did not catch him. The soul <note>original Greek: "psyche"</note> went beneath the earth like smoke,

"Oh, spirits! It is true then that even in the halls of Hades

ordered mules and men to fetch wood

# The Gathering of the Remains
## THE ILIAD

Those around the son of Atreus <note>Agamemnon, the leader of the Greek forces</note> gathered together in a crowd; the noise and thud of their approach woke Achilles from his sleep. He sat upright and spoke a word to them:
"Son of Atreus, and you other leaders of all the Achaeans <note>the Greeks</note>;
<margin>They extinguish the pyre with wine <note>original Latin: "Extingunt rogus vino"</note></margin>
first, extinguish the whole funeral pyre with sparkling wine, as far as the fury of the fire has spread. Afterward, let us gather the bones of Patroclus, son of Menoetius, distinguishing them clearly—and they are easy to recognize, for he lay in the very center of the pyre, while the others, horses and men mixed together, were burned at the edges. Let us place the bones in a golden bowl <note>original: "phiale," a broad, shallow vessel used for libations or holding precious items</note> and wrap them in a double layer of fat, until the time that I myself am hidden in the House of Hades <note>The underworld</note>. I do not command you to labor over a massive tomb, but only one that is fitting; later, you Achaeans may build it broad and high—those of you who are left behind me in the many-bench ships."

So he spoke, and they obeyed the swift-footed son of Peleus <note>Achilles</note>. First, they extinguished the funeral pyre with sparkling wine, as far as the flame had reached, and the deep ash fell in. Weeping, they gathered the white bones of their gentle companion into a golden bowl and a double layer of fat; they placed it in the hut and covered it with a soft linen cloth. Then they marked the circle of the tomb and laid down the foundation stones around the pyre; immediately after, they piled up the poured earth.
<margin>Funeral games <note>original Latin: "Ludi funebres"</note></margin>
When they had heaped up the burial mound, they started to leave. But Achilles restrained the people there and made them sit in a wide assembly. # THE ARGUMENT OF THE TWENTY-FOURTH 
# BOOK OF HOMER’S POEM

Zeus, taking pity on Hector, sends Thetis to Achilles so that he might return the body of the hero; and he sends Iris to Priam, so that by bringing a ransom to Achilles, he might 
<margin>putting to sleep <note>original: "κοι μι", likely a truncated reference to Hermes lulling the guards to sleep</note></margin>
recover the corpse of his son. Priam, escorted by Hermes and having lulled the Greek guards to sleep, arrives before Achilles. After entreating him, he receives back his son, and having carried him back to the city, he buries him, and in his honor, holds a funeral feast.

Let no thought of death or fear trouble his mind, for we shall grant him such a guide as the <term>Argeiphontes</term> <note>A title for the god Hermes, often translated as 'the slayer of Argus.'</note> <margin>the word "we shall grant" was provided <note>original Greek/Latin: "ὀπάσομεν praebuit"; a philological note regarding the verb tense used in the manuscript.</note></margin> who will lead him until he brings him close to Achilles. And when he has led him into the hut of Achilles, the hero will not kill him, and he will hold back all others; <note>Line 20 is underlined in red ink in the manuscript.</note> for he is not senseless, nor blind, nor a transgressor, but will spare a suppliant man with all kindness."
So he spoke, and storm-footed Iris rose to deliver the message. She reached the house of Priam and found there the sound of wailing and lamentation. The sons were sitting around their father inside the courtyard, soaking their clothes with tears. In their midst, the old man sat huddled, wrapped tightly in his cloak; and much filth lay upon the head and neck of the old man, which he had gathered with his own hands as he rolled upon the ground. Throughout the house, his daughters and his sons' wives were wailing.

Immediately he rose from his throne; he raised the old man by the hand,

<margin>Compassion and Humanity</margin>
"Ah, unhappy man, indeed you have endured many evils in your heart.

<margin>Achilles explains the human condition</margin>
For there is no profit in chilling <gloss>useless mourning</gloss> lamentation.
For this is the fate the gods have spun for wretched mortals:
to live in sorrow, while they themselves are free from care.
<margin>Two jars in the house of Zeus</margin>
For two jars sit upon the floor of Zeus <note>original: "Διὸς" - Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>,
containing the gifts he gives—one of evils, the other of blessings.
To whomsoever Zeus, the lover of thunder, gives a mingled lot,
that man meets now with evil, and now with good.
But to whom he gives only of the bitter lot, he makes him an object of shame;
<margin>Great hunger and calamity</margin>
and a foul <gloss>hunger</gloss> stinging misery <note>original: "βούβρωστις" (boubrōstis) - literally a 'ox-hunger' or a consuming plague that drives a person across the earth.</note> drives him over the divine earth,
and he wanders honored neither by gods nor by mortals.
<margin>How this argument applies</margin>
So too the gods gave shining gifts to Peleus from his birth;
for he excelled all men in wealth and riches,
and he ruled over the Myrmidons;
and though he was a mortal, they gave him a goddess <note>The sea-nymph Thetis.</note> for a wife.

<margin>Old age in his presence</margin>

far from my fatherland, bringing grief to you and your children.
And you, old man, we hear were once blessed..."

he drove them swiftly through the camp himself, and no one noticed. 
But when they reached the ford of the fair-flowing river, 
eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begat, 
Hermes then departed for high Olympus. 
And saffron-robed Dawn was spreading over all the earth; 
they drove the horses toward the city with wailing and 
groaning, and the mules carried the dead man. Nor did anyone 
else among the well-belted men and women recognize them 
before Cassandra, who, like golden Aphrodite, 
had climbed the height of Pergamus <note>The citadel or highest point of Troy.</note> and caught sight of her dear father. 
She saw him standing in the chariot with the herald, the city-crier; 
then she saw him <note>Hector.</note> who lay upon the bier on the mule-cart. 
At this, she shrieked and cried aloud throughout the whole city: 
"Come, men and women of Troy, and look upon Hector, 
if ever you rejoiced while he was still alive and 
returning from battle; for he was a great joy to the city and all its people!"
<margin>The city rushes together in mourning <note>original: "Concursatio et luctus per urbem"</note>.</margin>
So she spoke; and then not a single man or woman was left 
there in the city; for unbearable grief came upon them all. 
They met Priam near the gates as he brought the dead man in. 
First, his dear wife <note>Andromache.</note> and his lady mother <note>Hecuba.</note> 
rushed to the well-wheeled wagon, pulling at their hair 
as they touched his head; and the wailing crowd stood around them. 
And now they would have wept before the gates the whole 
day long until the sun went down, 
had the old man not spoken to the people from his chariot: 
"Make way for the mules to pass through; afterwards, 
you shall have your fill of weeping, once I have brought him home."

<summary>Hermes guides Priam safely out of the Greek camp to the river Xanthus before returning to Olympus. Cassandra is the first to spot her father returning with Hector's body, sparking a massive outpouring of grief as the entire city of Troy gathers at the gates to meet the funeral procession.</summary>

will seize you by the hand and hurl you from the wall <note>The walls of Troy.</note> to a grim death, 
venting his anger because Hector perhaps killed his brother, 
or his father, or his son; since very many Achaeans 
bit the vast earth with their teeth at the hands of Hector. 
For your father was not gentle in the grim heat of battle; 
therefore the people mourn him throughout the city. 
You have brought unspeakable wailing and grief to your parents, 
Hector; but for me, especially, bitter pains will remain. 
For as you died, you did not stretch out your hands to me from your bed, 
nor did you speak any final, meaningful word to me that I might 
always remember, night and day, through my falling tears." 
So she spoke, weeping; and the women wailed in response.

And among the women, Hecuba in turn led the vehement lamentation:

<margin>The Lament of Hecuba <note>original: "Planctus Hecubae"</note></margin>
> "Hector, to my soul by far the dearest of all my children,
> truly while you were alive you were dear to the gods;
> and they cared for you even in the destiny of death.
> For my other sons, swift-footed Achilles would sell as slaves, 
> whomever he captured, across the unresting sea,
> to Samos and Imbros and smoky Lemnos.
> But when he took away your life with the long-edged bronze <note>A reference to a bronze-tipped spear.</note>,
> he dragged you many times around the tomb of his comrade 
> Patroclus, whom you slew; yet even so he did not raise him up <note>Meaning the desecration of Hector's body could not bring Patroclus back to life.</note>.
> But now you lie for me in the halls, fresh and dewy <note>A sign of divine preservation; despite being dragged, Hector's body remained unblemished.</note>,
> like one whom silver-bowed Apollo has visited 
> and slain with his gentle arrows."

So she spoke, weeping, and stirred up endless wailing.

And then Helen, the third, led the mourning among them:

<margin>The Mourning of Helen <note>original: "Luctus Helenae"</note></margin>
> "Hector, to my soul by far the dearest of all my brothers-in-law;
> truly my husband is godlike Alexander <note>The prince also known as Paris, who took Helen from Sparta.</note>,
> who brought me to Troy—would that I had died before then!
> For this is now the twentieth year for me 
> since I came from there and left my native land.
> But never yet have I heard from you an evil or insulting word.
> Instead, if any other in the palace rebuked me—
<margin>A brother's wife <note>original: "Uxor fratris"</note></margin>
> —whether a brother-in-law, or a sister-in-law, or a brother's well-robed wife,
<margin>Mother-in-law <note>original: "Socrus"</note></margin>
> —or my mother-in-law (for my father-in-law <note>King Priam.</note> was always as kind as a father),
> you would restrain them, winning them over with your words,
> with your gentle spirit and your gentle speech.
> Therefore I wail for both you and my own ill-fated self, grieving at heart;
> for there is no one else left for me in wide Troy
> who is kind or a friend; but everyone shudders at me."

-># THE ILIAD<-

...the palace should upbraid me—whether it were any of your brothers or sisters, or your brothers’ well-dressed wives, or your mother (for your father was always as kind as a father)—you would restrain them with your words, with your gentleness and your gentle speech. Therefore I wail for you and for my own unhappy self with grief in my heart; for there is no one else left in wide Troy who is kind or friendly to me, but all shudder at me." <note>Helen concludes the series of three laments—by Andromache, Hecuba, and herself—highlighting Hector's unique character as a protector even of the woman who brought war to his city.</note>

So she spoke weeping, and the vast crowd of people wailed in response. Then the old man Priam spoke his word to the people:

"Bring wood now, Trojans, into the city, and do not fear in your hearts a thick-set ambush of the Greeks <note>original: "Ἀργείων" (Argives), one of the primary names Homer uses for the Greek forces.</note>; for Achilles, when he sent me back from the black ships, promised me that he would not harm us until the twelfth dawn comes."

So he spoke; and they yoked oxen and mules to wagons, and quickly they gathered before the city. For nine days they brought in a boundless supply of wood; but when the tenth dawn appeared, bringing light to mortals, they carried out brave Hector, shedding tears, and they placed the body upon the top of the funeral pyre and cast fire upon it.

And when the early-born, rosy-fingered Dawn <note>A famous Homeric "epithet" or recurring description for the sunrise.</note> appeared, then the people gathered around the pyre of famous Hector. But when they had assembled and come together, first they quenched the whole funeral pyre with gleaming wine <note>original: "αἴθοπι οἴνῳ" (aithopi oinō), referring to the dark, sparkling appearance of the wine.</note>, as far as the fire's fury had spread; then his brothers and comrades gathered the white bones, mourning, and a great tear flowed down their cheeks. 

And they took the bones and placed them in a golden casket <note>original: "λάρνακα" (larnaka), a chest used for remains.</note>, covering it with soft purple robes. Quickly then they placed it in a hollow grave, and from above, they covered it over with large, close-set stones. Swiftly they heaped up the burial mound; and watchers sat on every side, lest the well-armored Greeks <note>original: "ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί" (well-greaved Achaeans), referring to the bronze leg-protectors worn by the Greek soldiers.</note> should attack before the time was up. Having heaped the mound, they went back; and then, after gathering together, they feasted on a glorious banquet in the halls of Priam, the king nurtured by Zeus.

Thus they performed the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses.
